revision_paragraphs: Histopathology images are important for clinical diagnosis and disease prognosis. Although deep-learning methods have achieved comparable or surpassing performance relative to human pathologists’ reviewing in some histopathology-analysis tasks [2, 13, 28, 50], these methods typically require many detailed annotations. Such annotations require experienced pathologists, are costly and time-consuming to obtain, and can contain human errors. This challenge is particularly acute for histopathology images because of their large size and the irregular shapes of target tissues (Figure 1). We address partially supervised histopathology segmentation from in-target and out-of-target point annotations, a setting in which existing approaches designed for natural images or medical images with relatively regular objects and consistent textures are often not directly applicable. In contrast to consistency-training approaches based on data augmentation [15, 30], we introduce a contrast-based variational model that uses correlations with both in-target and out-of-target points to provide complementary supervision. We show through experiments on two histology datasets that this model is effective and efficient relative to previous models, while its contrast-map construction helps address unlabeled novel tissue regions.

We focus on partially supervised histopathology segmentation using in-target and out-of-target point annotations, where in-target points lie inside target regions and out-of-target points lie outside them. Histopathology images differ substantially from other image types. In many such images, target objects have distinctive regional characteristics: as illustrated in Figure 1, tumors can cluster in large regions with similar morphological features or textures that differ visually from surrounding regions and have comparatively clear boundaries. Existing partially supervised methods do not explicitly exploit these characteristics. In addition, a tissue section can contain non-target regions whose visual or morphological properties differ from those seen in other images. When these regions are unlabeled, they are novel to a trained model, and their predicted categories depend on their similarity to neutral and target tissues. Novel regions that resemble target tissues can therefore be predicted as target, producing false detections. This issue can be particularly challenging for methods based on consistency training with data augmentation [15, 30], because consistency supervision can reinforce these errors.
